extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in religion, deism, and rational critique of scripture (readers of Thomas Paine)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing the truth, origin, and moral effects of revealed religion and sacred texts from a deist/rationalist perspective; emphasizes evidence from nature, internal consistency, and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief must be founded on facts visible in the creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief of a future state is a rational belief, founded upon facts visible in the creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paine argues that belief in a future state is no harder to accept than natural transformations (worm to butterfly) when based on observable facts; favor empirical, creation-based evidence over purely textual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revelation is only personal divine communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelation can only be applied to something which God reveals of his will to the person to whom it is made; the account of it to another is not revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept secondhand testimony as revelation. The proper stance is: 'When it is revealed to me, I will believe it to be revelation.' This rejects treating someone else's claim as divine communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take the word of man for the word of God
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not proper that I should take the word of man as the word of God, or put man in the place of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptically evaluate claims framed as divine revelation if their authority rests on human testimony, tradition, or institutional decree rather than direct, verifiable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural evidence must be coherent and not self-contradictory
rubrics_metrics.description: The contradictory impossibilities contained in the Old Testament and the New ... put them in the case of a man who swears for and against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal contradictions or mutually exclusive statements in sacred texts undermine their authenticity; evidence drawn from scriptures must be consistent and not 'swear for and against' itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and explanatory power are required (avoid meaningless jargon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that explain nothing and illustrate nothing (the 'doubtful jargon' ascribed to Paul) are destitute of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments or passages that leave the reader without clear meaning are an anti-pattern. Favor propositions that clarify, explain, or illuminate rather than obscure or confound the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogies and metaphors must be valid and pertinent
rubrics_metrics.description: An improper metaphor (e.g., Paul's sowing/grain metaphor) that confuses succession with resurrection is not a true simile and is misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that analogies accurately parallel the point being argued; invalid or inapt metaphors weaken theological arguments and should not be treated as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology must rest on demonstrable principles and data
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of theology as it stands in Christian churches ... is founded on nothing; it has no data; it can demonstrate nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate theological claims should be grounded in principles that can be demonstrated or supported by observable facts (the 'Bible of the creation' / science), not on contested textual assertions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality is not proof of divine revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the morality of an account would be no proof of revelation; moral fragments in scripture are natural dictates of conscience, not evidence of divine origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept moral goodness of a text or teaching as evidence that it is divinely revealed; morality can arise from conscience and common social principles independent of claimed revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural theology (creation as authoritative text)
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation is the Bible of the deist. He there reads ... the certainty of his existence, and the immutability of his power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the observable universe, scientific principles, and the regularity of nature as the primary sources for understanding the Creator and grounding religious belief rather than depending on human-authored scriptures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of beliefs weakens conviction; favor simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of a Trinity of Gods has enfeebled the belief of one God. A multiplication of beliefs acts as a division of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal complexity or multiplication of entities/claims dilutes rational belief; simpler, unified doctrines are more coherent and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral maxims must be clear, defined, and practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral maxims should always be clear and defined; vague terms like 'enemies' make precepts meaningless and impracticable (critique of 'love your enemies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical prescriptions for specificity and possibility of performance; avoid duties that are vague, impossible, or that would produce perverse incentives (e.g., 'love your enemies' as a duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties prescribed by religion must be possible and not incentivize harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality is injured by prescribing duties that are impossible to be performed, and if they could be would be productive of evil; loving enemies would be a premium for crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject moral obligations that cannot be reasonably fulfilled or that would encourage wrongdoing; assess duties for feasibility and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate religions by their historical social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The most detestable wickedness, the most horrid cruelties ... have had their origin in this thing called revelation, or revealed religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the track record of a religion—persecutions, wars, atrocities—as evidence for judging the moral and social validity of claims of revealed authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human institutional authority (votes/councils) does not confer divine authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: It was upon the vote of such as Athanasius that the Testament was decreed to be the word of God; nothing can present a more strange idea than that of decreeing the word of God by vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat canonical status derived from councils, political power, or human voting with skepticism; human consensus alone is not proof of divine origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious claims should not contradict immutable laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher knows that the laws of the Creator have never changed ... Why then is it to be supposed they have changed with respect to man?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological assertions that imply a change in the immutable laws observable in nature are suspect; prefer interpretations consistent with natural laws and scientific understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force belief; belief must remain voluntary and rational
rubrics_metrics.description: We should never force belief upon ourselves in any thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief formed under compulsion or habit is unreliable; encourage free inquiry and leave acceptance to rational conviction rather than coercion or social pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific and practical texts ('Bible of the creation') for theological instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of science ... is a text as well for devotion as for philosophy—for gratitude, as for human improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors and preachers should employ scientific knowledge and practical arts to cultivate reverence and moral improvement rather than relying solely on contested scriptural texts; houses of devotion could function as schools of science.
